Shares of Chevron (CVX) rose 1.8% on October 30, 2026, the day the company reported fiscal Q3 2026 results, while the S&P 500 fell 1.8%. By November 6, the stock had fallen 8.1% from its close before the report, compared with a 4.4% decline for the index. Profit fell from the second quarter, yet it remained nearly three times its level a year earlier. So what is Chevron doing with the extra money? On the October 30 call, management said Chevron cut its debt by more than $3 billion in the quarter and added more than $4 billion to its cash. Buybacks did not rise alongside those moves. Management said the company kept its buyback rate at $2.5 billion to $3 billion and intends to stay within that range. Chevron bought back $11.1 billion of shares in the four quarters to September. On report day, Chevron’s advance slightly trailed the gains at Exxon Mobil and ConocoPhillips, which rose 2.2% and 2.7%. Over the past twelve months, Chevron’s free cash flow equaled 8.2% of its market value, while its dividends and buybacks together totaled 6.0%. The company is retaining more cash than it hands back, and its debt has declined. Total debt stood at $33.5 billion at the end of September, compared with $41.5 billion a year earlier. Has Chevron’s Bigger Profit Lasted More Than Two Quarters? Not yet. Chevron earned $2.21 billion in the first quarter of 2026, before profit jumped to $12.1 billion in the second quarter and settled at $9.92 billion in the third. On management’s own measure, adjusted earnings were $10.4 billion, down $1.6 billion from the second quarter. Management said upstream earnings fell on lower prices and lower volumes sold, while downstream earnings rose on higher refining margins and volumes. Chevron has earned profit this high before, and it faded. Since 2021, only the twelve months to September 2022, at $34.2 billion, brought more profit than the latest twelve-month stretch. Profit then fell in each of the years to September 2023, 2024 and 2025. Investors now pay 15.4 times the past twelve months’ earnings for the shares, compared with 21.8 for the S&P 500, and those twelve months include both big quarters. What Did Chevron’s Management Say About The Months Ahead? Management said Chevron will not change how it spends cash while prices swing this widely. Prices ranged from as low as $68 to as high as $132 a barrel within the third quarter, so the company is changing nothing in the short term, and growing the dividend stays its first priority. On refining, management expects margins to stay elevated in the short term, with 10% of the world’s refining capacity offline. It also called refining and chemical margins very difficult to predict. Chevron said turnarounds and downtime would cut its fourth-quarter upstream output by 175,000 to 225,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day. The fourth quarter brings one known charge. Management expects a transaction to close at the end of the quarter that takes $3.7 billion of debt off Chevron’s books and lifts its Bakken upstream earnings in 2027. Chevron will then report a one-time non-cash loss of $3 billion to $4 billion, a special item management said reflects only the accounting. With that loss set apart, the figure to watch when Chevron reports in January 2027 is fourth-quarter adjusted earnings, against $10.4 billion in the third quarter. title: One Unsettled Question Sits Under Chevron Stock - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. Chevron (CVX) could lose some of what it earns from making fuel once a global shortage of refining capacity eases. During its October 30, 2026 call, management said 10% of the world’s refining capacity was offline at the time. Chevron’s own U.S. refineries, by contrast, ran a record amount of crude in the third quarter. You cannot yet tell how much of Chevron’s business is exposed to that shortage. A refining margin is the difference between what a refiner pays for crude oil and what it collects for the fuel it makes. Chevron’s refining operations sit in its Downstream business. Management said adjusted downstream earnings rose in the third quarter from the second because of higher refining margins and volumes. The whole company did not follow suit. Adjusted earnings fell by $1.6 billion from the second quarter, as upstream earnings dropped on lower realizations and lower liftings. A question about global supply, including how much capacity is offline worldwide, came up on that October 30 call. Downstream brought in $142 billion of revenue in fiscal 2025, against $88.4 billion for Upstream. Segment revenue can include sales between Chevron’s own businesses, however, and revenue alone does not show what each business earns. Downstream revenue fell 9.8% that year. Across the whole company, the operating margin is now wider than a year ago. The operating margin reached 17.5% in the third quarter of 2026, up from 8.9% in the third quarter of 2025. Over the past twelve months it was 14.6%. That level is higher than at 34 of the 40 quarter ends since the end of 2016, so the company is earning near the top of its own ten-year range. Management has said it expects refining margins to stay elevated in the short term. It expects those margins to moderate as refinery runs recover and export flows increase, a process management said will take some time. On chemicals, management put the share of petrochemical capacity offline at between 5% and 10%, and said margins will likely stay a bit elevated at least through the end of the year, maybe into 2027. Management also said that without some capacity closures and project deferrals, the chemicals market may return to oversupply as flows normalize. In both cases, management tied the easing to supply coming back. Chevron is adding capacity of its own, including roughly 15% more at its Pasadena refinery and another 7% planned at Pascagoula by 2030. These additions give the company more fuel to sell at whatever margin the market pays. In its fourth-quarter report, expected in January 2027, the figure to watch is whether Chevron’s downstream earnings rise or fall from the third quarter’s.
